name: Ethics and Bias Audit Projects
title: Ethics and Bias Audit Projects
answer: Ethics and bias audit projects have older students test real AI tools with carefully chosen inputs to see whether different groups are treated differently, then write up findings and propose fixes. They matter because they show that AI tools are made by people and can be questioned and improved, and the book reports research from middle schools that students can handle this work.

sections.body: An ethics and bias audit project is a structured activity in which students examine a real AI tool for signs that it treats different groups differently. Students choose inputs carefully, observe the tool's outputs, and look for patterns that may disadvantage or exclude some people. They then write up what they found and suggest changes that could make the tool fairer. The idea addresses the problem that AI tools can carry bias and that students may otherwise treat them as neutral or beyond question. By doing the audit themselves, students learn that these tools are built by people and can be inspected, challenged, and improved.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: With older students, a bias audit project asks them to test a real AI tool using carefully chosen inputs and observe whether different groups get different treatment. They might examine an image generator to see whether it shows only certain kinds of people for roles like doctor or engineer, then write up findings and propose fixes. In middle school, the book says students can handle this work, and one workshop had them learn how machine learning works, identify bias, suggest ways to reduce it, and connect AI to future careers. High school students can take the same ideas further. The teacher reviews the plan before students begin.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book presents this idea under the label of research from middle schools showing students can handle this work. It cites Zhang et al., 2023, for a workshop in which middle school students learned how machine learning works, identified bias in AI systems, suggested ways to reduce it, and connected AI to future careers. It cites Williams et al., 2023, for three AI and ethics curricula for middle school, where trained teachers could teach them well using active learning and ethics woven into technical lessons. The text gives no other figures or studies for this idea.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits: bias audits must use tools that meet student age limits. Students should work only with approved tools, remove any personal information from their tests, and avoid generating harmful content even to study it. The teacher reviews the plan before students begin. The decisions about which tools are approved, what inputs are acceptable, and when a plan is ready stay with the teacher. Done carefully, these projects teach students that AI tools are made by people and can be questioned and improved.
